title: Fitting kitchen cornice and pelmet rail
subtitle: Mitre and fix decorative cornice moulding to the top of wall cabinets and a pelmet rail to the underside, giving a furniture-built-in look
excerpt: How to fit kitchen cornice moulding to the top of wall units and a pelmet rail to the underside. Covers cutting internal and external mitres, fixing to the cabinet faces, and filling the joints.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK kitchen-fitting trade practice. Newey and Drage, Practical Carpentry and Joinery (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A decorative moulding fitted to the top of wall-mounted kitchen cabinets, projecting forward to give the appearance of traditional cabinet-maker's cornice. Usually supplied in the same finish as the cabinet doors. Available in straight runs and in pre-cut corner blocks for internal and external corners.

A moulded rail fitted to the underside of wall cabinets to finish the cabinet base line and to conceal under-cabinet lighting. Usually 40-60 mm tall and supplied to match the cornice and door profile.

content.text: give wall units a built-in, furniture quality. The job is cut the mitres accurately and fix the runs tightly to the cabinet faces. The power mitre saw makes consistent repeatable cuts; the hand saw and mitre box are a workable substitute for a small kitchen.
Measure and plan the cornice run

Note every internal and external corner in the cabinet run. For internal corners (a wall-to-wall run), the two meeting pieces each get a 45-degree cut that close together. For external corners (a projecting cabinet end), the two pieces mitre outward at 45 degrees. Measure each run from the inside of one corner to the inside of the next. Add 20 mm per mitre for waste.

Set the mitre saw to 45 degrees. The cornice profile has a flat back and a shaped face; hold it against the saw fence with the back face flat. Cut a dry-run set first and check the fit before gluing. Kitchen corners are rarely a perfect 90 degrees; adjust the mitre angle by 1-2 degrees if the joint shows a gap. Cut the straight runs to length with a square end.
Fix the cornice to the cabinet tops

Apply a bead of PVA wood glue to the back face of the cornice where it contacts the cabinet. Drive 40 mm panel pins through the face of the cornice into the cabinet carcase at 300 mm intervals. Punch the pin heads just below the surface. Hold the mitre joints while the glue sets by wrapping with masking tape for 30 minutes. Check the run is level before the glue goes off.

The pelmet rail fits to the underside of the wall units with the same method: mitre the corners, glue and pin to the cabinet base. The pelmet run usually stops at the ends of the cabinets without a return, unless the end is visible from the room. Fill all pin holes, sand lightly, and paint to match the cabinet finish.

attrs.symptom: Mitre joint at internal corner shows a triangular gap at the wall side
attrs.cause: The cabinet run is not square to the wall, so the effective angle at the corner is more or less than 90 degrees.
attrs.fix: Adjust the mitre to bisect the actual corner angle (measure with a sliding bevel) or use pre-cut corner blocks supplied with many kitchen ranges.

attrs.symptom: Cornice pulls away from the cabinet at the pin positions after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Pins too short, or the PVA was not applied across the full contact face.
attrs.fix: Re-fix with longer pins (50 mm) and re-apply PVA to any loose sections, clamping with masking tape while the glue sets.
